content_html_sanitized:
Posted May 28, 2002
Analysis by Richard Cowan

The New York Times and The Washington Post have not yet told their readers about the change in UK cannabis policies.
See

However, the Times to its great credit editorialized Friday against the Federal government's efforts to censor conversations between doctors and their patients about medical cannabis. The case is now before the 9th Circuit of the Federal Appeals court in San Francisco, where we are virtually certain to prevail.
See

It is very significant that the Times editorial did not just make the First Amendment argument that the Federal government has no business interfering in conversations between doctors and patients.

" The federal policy also clashes with the free-speech protections of the First Amendment. The federal government wants to punish physicians merely for advising a patient about the benefits of marijuana. That restriction infringes directly on the First Amendment right of doctors to speak freely and, no less important, the right of patients to receive the best possible medical information. "

It would have been very easy for the Times to confine its arguments to the free-speech issues, so it is politically important that they specifically supported the evidence for the medical use of cannabis.

We are also likely to prevail if the Feds appeal to the Supreme Court. I think that they know that they will lose, but they are persisting in order to intimidate doctors so they will be afraid even to discuss cannabis with their patients, even though the Feds are under a restraining order and the doctors have every right to do so, until the Supreme Court rules otherwise.

The Feds obvious purpose is to undermine the various state medical marijuana laws that exempt patients from state but not federal marijuana laws if they have some kind of doctor recommendation for cannabis. Federal laws prohibit prescribing a Schedule I drug, so the state medical marijuana laws allow doctors to merely " recommend " cannabis. There is no resulting prescription, but without some sort of doctor's approval, the state laws would be unworkable. This approval is the result of private conversations between the doctor and the patient. In short, there is no public component to the speech.

Meanwhile, the Washington Post has not been so enthusiastic about medical cannabis. Indeed, the editors just " don't get it. "
See

Today's Post has an Op-ed,

According to Schultz and Taylor, the FDA is urging the public and the pharmaceutical industries " to supply it with arguments about whether the First Amendment to the Constitution limits the FDA's power over advertising. even when important public health interests are at stake. " In short, the Administration is trying to undermine its power over the drug companies, even as it reaches for more power over the patients.

" The FDA is asking whether the agency's authority is limited by a constitutional right of businesses to promote drugs and other products for uses that have never been proven. "

Of course, the same administration is attacking medical cannabis suppliers, because the same government that has blocked medical testing of cannabis says that is unproven.

So here we have the Bush administration trying to censor private speech about cannabis and loosen restrictions on advertising on pharmaceuticals. Of course, when George Bush was a candidate, he said that the issue of medical cannabis should be left up to the states. He has done just the opposite, so trying to censor doctors is hardly surprising.
See

Schultz and Taylor conclude by saying, " Americans take it for granted that drug and other health-product companies should be required to demonstrate the safety and effectiveness of their products before they promote them. These common-sense assumptions are now being questioned by government lawyers who argue that the First Amendment to the Constitution severely limits the government's role in monitoring commercial speech about products with serious health consequences. It is hard to imagine that this was the intent of the Founders in 1789 or is in the public's interest today. "

There is a great irony in the reference to the Founders in any attempt to strength the authority of the Federal government.

In fact, what has happened is that well-intentioned laws, ostensibly designed to protect the public against the depredations of the pharmaceutical companies, are being used to attack patients who choose to use a plant rather than the pharmaceutical companies products.

Schultz and Taylor make interesting arguments for preserving federal power, but it is impossible to trust an institution capable of perverting the Constitution, the laws and their own campaign promises. Readers of the Washington Post would be the last to understand these doubts. The Post, like the FDA, is supposed to protect the rights of the people. The First Amendment protects them, but it is also supposed to protect us all.
